lesson.title: Z-Scores: Measuring Distance in Standard Deviations
lesson.summary: A z-score converts a raw value into the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean, giving a standardized way to describe how unusual or typical a value is.
lesson.body:
A z-score answers a question that neither the mean nor the standard deviation answers on its own: exactly how far, in a standardized sense, does one particular value sit from the center of its distribution? The formula is z equals x minus the mean, all divided by the standard deviation. The numerator, x minus the mean, is the same deviation used to build standard deviation and variance; the z-score simply rescales that deviation by dividing by the standard deviation, converting the distance into units of number of standard deviations instead of the original units.

This rescaling is what makes z-scores so useful. A deviation of 8 points might be enormous in a data set where the standard deviation is 2, but tiny in a data set where the standard deviation is 50. By dividing the deviation by the standard deviation, the z-score expresses distance from the mean in a common, unit free scale: a z-score of 2 always means the same thing, two standard deviations above the mean, regardless of whether the original data were measured in dollars, seconds, or test points.

Return once more to the data set 4, 8, 6, 5, and 3, with mean 5.2 and sample standard deviation approximately 1.92. To find the z-score of the value 8, subtract the mean from the value: 8 minus 5.2 equals 2.8. Then divide by the standard deviation: 2.8 divided by 1.92 is approximately 1.46. So the value 8 has a z-score of about 1.46, meaning it sits roughly 1.46 standard deviations above the mean of this particular data set.

The sign of a z-score always tells you direction, positive means above the mean, negative means below it, while the magnitude tells you distance in standard deviation units. A z-score of 0 means the value equals the mean exactly. Values close to 0 are typical for their distribution, while values with large positive or large negative z-scores are farther from the center and, depending on the shape of the distribution, potentially unusual. A negative z-score is not a bad thing and a positive z-score is not automatically a good thing; the sign only tells you which side of the mean a value falls on, and whether that side is desirable depends entirely on what is being measured, such as a low round time in a race versus a low test score.

Because a z-score depends on both the mean and the standard deviation, and neither of those is resistant to outliers, z-scores inherit that same sensitivity: an outlier in the data set can distort the mean and standard deviation used to compute every other value's z-score, sometimes even making an outlier's own z-score look smaller than it should because the outlier inflated the very standard deviation used to measure it. Still, the z-score is one of the most powerful tools in statistics precisely because it strips away the original units and lets you compare values from completely different distributions on the same standardized scale, a process explored fully under standardization and put to direct use when comparing values with z-scores.
